doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Friendship after Riverside, Fantasy, and Cannonball as producer
summary: They stayed close until reuniting at Fantasy in 1973, and Cannonball produced records including Budd Johnson's.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: Cannonball, who was coming near the end of his Capitol contract and Capitol wasn’t doing anything in jazz at that point. And so Cannonball and I ended up together at Fantasy for what turned out to be the last few years of his life. But in that intervening period between 1964 when Riverside died, and 1973 when we both were together at Fantasy, in that period we remained close personal friends. And we saw a lot of each other, we talked to each other a lot, we shared non-musical things, and that I have to say is among the handful of things that I feel best about, in my career. So I hope that’s some kind of an answer to what I think about Cannonball Adderley. And this was among the things that he insisted on doing, and did some very valuable work in — I’d say he was my star pupil. I mean he became a producer, there was a whole series of “Cannonball Adderley Presents” which were pretty evenly divided between his trying to resurrect the careers of neglected older players, or he was trying to discover new players. Chuck Mangione’s first record was made — I don’t know whether Cannon should get credit for that or otherwise — but no Chuck was a damn good player. And he did a wonderful record with Cleanhead Vinson. And he did a wonderful record with Budd Johnson. You talk about underrated tenor players. There’s a wonderful Budd Johnson record on Riverside called “Budd Johnson and the Four Brass Giants.” The idea was let’s do Budd Johnson with a trumpet section. Cannon put this thing together with his dates for the trumpet section was Sweets Edison, Clark Terry, Nat Adderley and oh God the Ellington trumpet player who also played wonderful violin.
Ray Nance. Ray was the fourth trumpet player and doubled violin on a couple of numbers. So that was a throw-away idea of his.
